en: If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified. (8.201)

He demonstrates the kind of purchase by which ownership arises: "Vikraya" refers to the marketplace (*āpaṇabhūmi*), where traders conduct their business. One who receives from there either the wealth consisting of cattle and the like, or the commodity being purchased, or the price, obtains it through a lawful purchase. It must be "pure in the presence of the community" (*kulasaṃnidhau viśuddham*). A "lawful purchase" means at an appropriate price. That which is received in the presence of a group of people (*kulasya*)—a crowd of other traders and brokers (*melakakāra*)—who are men whose guilt is not suspected, one obtains it and does not lose it. Otherwise, if the sale was made by one who is not the owner, the property must be returned; however, [the buyer] receives the price. Therefore, he who sold it is punished for the unlawful purchase and must forfeit the price. This is what has been stated.

"Upon seeing the seller, [the purchaser] is purified; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the purchaser obtains his money from whoever was the seller of that [article]. (YDh 2.174).
This very same point is established by this verse. 8.201.

Now, if the root source cannot be recovered, but the sale was proven to have been made openly and the goods were cleared of suspicion, the seller shall not be punished by the king and is released; the original owner recovers his property. (8.202)

The purchase from a person whose wickedness is improbable and so forth has been declared according to legal principle (*nyāyataḥ*). If that seller can be produced, then the previously mentioned rule applies, beginning with "The owner [recovers] the property" (YDh 2.174). Now, if that seller has disappeared, and the one by whom the item was purchased cannot produce the owner who marked it, nor can he produce the original seller; yet it was purchased openly in the presence of people at a well-known place of sale—then, when the property has been cleared by such a purchase, the purchaser is purified, is not to be punished, and is released. However, the owner who lost the property—the *nāṣṭika*—obtains his wealth, provided he has made himself known as the owner. The term *nāṣṭika* means "one who seeks what is lost" (*naṣṭam anveṣate*). By adding the suffix *ṭhan* to *naṣṭa*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the base itself because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group; or alternatively, it means "one for whom the lost thing is the purpose. Thus, the summary is this: "In the case of an open purchase, there shall be no punishment, but the loss of the wealth remains as it was. (8.202)
An object whose form is mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor should one that is defective, nor one that is deficient, nor one that is at a distance, nor one that is concealed. (8.203)

In connection with the topic of selling what does not belong to oneself (*asvāmivikraya*), other rules regarding sale are also stated. One must not sell another substance, such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and the like, mixed with a "bad substance" (*kudravya*) that merely resembles it, such as safflower (*kusumbha*). Furthermore, one must not sell that which is "defective" (*sāvadya*)—such as clothing and so forth—which, having been kept in a container for a long time, has lost its luster and become worn out, yet appears as if it were new; nor that which is "insufficient" in weight or measure. One must not sell that which is "remote," meaning situated at a distance in another village, saying, "I have clothing or substances such as molasses there"; nor that which is "concealed," meaning covered by cloth or the like, or whose true nature is hidden by some dyeing substance, or that which is old but appears as if new—that is "concealed" and should not be sold. A sale should be conducted after displaying the substance and its condition in this manner. If, however, it is done otherwise, the sale is not valid; even if the item is returned after ten days, there is no fault [on the part of the buyer].
Since no other punishment has been mentioned here, this punishment [is prescribed] by the words "by means of tests" (MDh 8.193);
others, however, maintain that because it is recited within a different section, it is the punishment for selling what one does not own. 8.203.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the groom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single bride-price.

Since the giving of a maiden by means of a fee (*śulka*) and so forth is a form of sale, the law regarding this matter is stated in this section: If one who has received a fee shows a beautiful girl at the time of the payment but then gives one who is deficient in beauty, deficient in age, or deficient in virtue, both [girls] must be taken back by the single fee-giver for that same fee. This rule applies specifically to maidens; however, in the case of goods such as cattle or horses, another rule will be stated for such a transgression. (8.204)

A giver does not deserve punishment if he has first declared the defects [of the girl], provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already experienced sexual intercourse. 8.205.

Having stated that there is no penalty for one who gives [a girl] after declaring defects such as insanity, the author states by way of prohibition the penalty for one who does not declare them. Not only should she not be given in exchange for a bride-price (*śulka*), but even if she has been given to another who intends to marry her through a *brāhma* or other form of marriage, she remains as if ungiven; and for one who knows [of the defect], he incurs the guilt of a thief (MDh 8.198). For one who does not know, the fine is six hundred, because that is the subject under discussion. [The defects are: those such as leprosy and insanity in the case of a girl who is insane or leprous; and the defect of a girl who has experienced sexual intercourse, namely the fact of having been touched in sexual union. Having previously made these defects known by verbal declaration, having revealed them, and having said, "This girl possesses such a defect," there is no penalty for one who gives her—this is the purpose [of the rule]. (8.205)
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should fail to perform his own duty,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the other performers together.

This is the introduction to the topic of collective enterprise (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*). In this regard, he first cites a Vedic example of collective work: the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others. In that context, for the purpose of accomplishing the various constituent rites of the sacrifice, a priest is chosen with the agreement: "By you, this office of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, or the *udgātṛ* must be performed," and it is undertaken as something to be executed according to the Vedic injunction. If, due to some incapacity or the like, one were to abandon or fail to complete what was half-done, then a share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to him in proportion to the work performed. Having determined the total fee for that sacrifice, a fourth part is given when a fourth of the rite is completed, a third when a third is completed, and so on; such is the proportionality. "Together with the performers": the performers are the subordinate priests (*tatpuruṣa*) of the principal officiants (*pradhānartvij*), such as the *hotṛ*, *udgātṛ*, and others—the *prastotṛ*, *maitrāvaruṇa*, and so forth. (8.206)
If, after the sacrificial fees have been distributed, one abandons his own work, he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another. (8.207)

"The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are given at the midday pressing. Therefore, after that point, one who abandons the ritual should receive the fee—which is the understood sense—that cannot be reclaimed; the meaning is that one should not cause the ritual to be abandoned prematurely. Having paid another wage, the sacrificer should have that ritual completed by another person. Since the ritual must be performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), they become such through their formal selection (*varaṇa*), and that [selection] occurs at a fixed time prior to the commencement of the rite. Consequently, the sacrifice being performed becomes defective, yet the completion must also be achieved; thus, it is stated "by another" in order to dispel the notion: "If it is defective, I shall complete it, performing the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) myself through other agents. Only that which is impossible is considered defective; however, everything that is possible must be performed.

Some authorities maintain that the term "should cause to be performed" implies a connection with officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). If the patron is unable to perform it himself, he may take the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and give an additional amount. Prior to the distribution of the fees, the patron alone is authorized to complete the remaining rites. (8.207)
In whatever rite specific fees for individual officiants have been prescribed, that very person shall receive them, or all may share them together. (8.208)

This other Vedic matter relevant to the present topic is now stated. In Vedic ritual, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are prescribed in their entirety, not divided per individual: "Its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve. And by extension (*atideśa*), that rule follows other sacrifices that are modifications of it, such as the *rājasūya* and others. In some of those subsidiary rites (*aṅgakarma*), however, a different fee is prescribed for each specific step in connection with a particular person: "Two golden mirrors for the *adhvaryu*" (Śabara on PMS 10.3.63), and so forth. These become the "fees for each subsidiary" (*pratyaṅgadakṣiṇā*). The purpose of this verse is to introduce a doubt: Is the connection with the act of giving (*dadāti*) like that of the four classes of priests (*cāturvidya-vādikavat*), such that the fees belong to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) while the *adhvaryu* is merely the channel; or rather, do they belong to him alone, while the others receive only their share from the original fee? "Fees for each subsidiary" (*pratyaṅgadakṣiṇā*) means fees for the subsidiaries that depend upon specific persons at each step. Alternatively, the word *prati* is used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*); thus *pratyaṅga* means "depending on limb after limb" (*aṅgam aṅgam āśritāḥ*). The question is: Should he alone take them, because the person is directly connected with the act of giving (*dadāti*)? Or, since there is no distinction in their status as performers (*kartṛtva*), should the others also partake and receive them, just as they do with the primary fee? Having raised this, the conclusion is stated: since specific persons have been mentioned in connection with the fees, they are intended for those persons alone. In this way, the verb "to give" (*dadāti*) retains its primary meaning, and the connection with the specific persons is not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). (8.208)
The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot, and the Brahman priest the horse at the formal gift;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase.

At the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires), the *adhvaryu* should take away a chariot; the *brahmā*, a swift horse; and the *hotṛ*, either a stallion or another horse. In some recensions of the *ādhāna*, these are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Therefore, at the purchase of the *soma*, the cart that is used belongs to the *udgātṛ*. It is also recorded that on that cart one ox should be yoked and the other unyoked; with that cart the purchased *soma* is brought forward. Others, however, say that the ox is not mentioned as something previously established for the purpose of bringing the *soma*, for it cannot be distinguished by the act of purchase itself. (8.209)

Thus, the rule for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of the limbs [of the victim] associated with specific persons has been stated. Now he describes the distribution of the principal sacrificial fees as they are generally prescribed:
"Of all [the priests], the chief ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
the third group are entitled to a third part; and those entitled to a fourth part receive a quarter. (8.210)

Among all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who are the principal ones are the *ardhins* (those entitled to half). Whatever total sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for that sacrifice as a whole, they are the recipients of its half; that is, they take the half. For in Soma sacrifices there are sixteen officiating priests, among whom four are principal: the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ. Half of their share is twelve hundred [coins], since the sacrificial fee is one thousand two hundred; thus, half of that is fifty-six [35]. By half of that [36], namely twenty-eight, are the *ardhins*; others possess this status, whose appointment immediately follows theirs: the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ [37]. The *tṛtīyins* are those entitled to a third part. The word *aṃśa* has the same meaning as the word *ardha*, and the word *ardha* does not necessarily denote an exactly equal division; rather, it applies by proximity even when there is a slight deficiency or excess. Therefore, a third part of the fifty-six is taken as sixteen; thus each of these four receives four. They give an equal third part: the fourth part of the fifty-six goes to the Acchāvāka of the Hotṛ, the Neṣṭṛ of the Adhvaryu, the Agnīdh of the Brahman, and the Pratihartṛ of the Udgātṛ. And those who are the *pādins* perform a fourth part of the work, and are thus called *pādins*. They occupy the fourth position at the end of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s place; they are entitled to a fourth part. In the group of twelve, it is as before. In this way, the distribution must also be made in the case of the rule: "They consecrate him with a hundred," using such expressions as "he consecrates the *ardhins*, he consecrates the *pādins*. In that context, the rule regarding the sequence of the twelve is indeed the same; the usage heard elsewhere is applied here according to that very method. (8.210)
When men here perform their respective duties in combination, the apportionment of their shares must be determined by this application of the rule. (8.211)

Just as in a sacrifice, he who is appointed to many tasks that cause bodily hardship and require exceptional skill receives a larger sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), while one who performs fewer tasks receives less; in the same way, among those engaged in worldly undertakings such as building a house or a temple—among carpenters, master builders, architects, and so forth—the share of each is established according to their own convention. By this application of rule (*vidhiyogena*)—where "rule" means the Vedic purpose and its established arrangement—the meaning is: by the Vedic arrangement pertaining to the sacrifice. Likewise, in the viewing of a drama and the like, there is an apportionment of shares among the dancers, singers, and musicians. Even though all are learned and capable of performing every task, the share is according to the nature of the work and not according to the person; such is the undertaking by association (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*). (8.211)
If wealth has been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of Dharma, but that wealth does not subsequently serve that purpose, then it should not have been given to him. (8.212)

If someone says, "I am a member of a religious community (*sāntānika*), or I intend to perform a sacrifice; give me something," and if [the gift] were given to him, he might not perform the sacrifice nor engage in the rites of marriage. He might squander that wealth on gambling or with prostitutes, or employ it elsewhere for interest, profit, agriculture, and so forth. It should not be given to such a person. Therefore, the prohibition of giving to him does not logically apply to what has already been given; hence, the meaning of the sentence is that it must be recovered. Alternatively, the word *datta* (given) should be explained in its secondary sense (*gauṇa*): what is promised (*pratiśruta*) but not yet given is not to be given. And thus Gautama says: "Even after promising, one should not give to one who is unrighteous" (GDh 5.23). What, then, is appropriate here? He says: both. That is, the recovery of what has been given, or the non-giving of what was promised. Accordingly, both are recited in another Smṛti. For Nārada says, beginning with "I shall perform this rite": "What may have been given through ignorance is considered as not given" (NSm 4.9–10). When something has been given for a specific purpose, if that purpose is not accomplished, it must be taken back from the house of the recipient even if it has already been settled. At that time, the handing over is merely the commencement of the gift; the completion occurs when the purpose is fulfilled—this is the opinion of Nārada. (8.212)
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed, he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft. (8.213)

*Saṃsādhana* (recovery) consists of seeking out what was promised like a debt through reporting it to the king and so forth; or, when what was accepted is being demanded back, reporting it to the king, saying: "Having given this to me, he wishes to take it back. *Saṃsādhana* is the strengthening of what has been established. [47] The phrase "out of pride or greed" is a restatement of the cause. For one who acts in this way, the fine shall be gold; this is the atonement (*niṣkṛti*) for that theft. [48] Anticipating the suspicion of a thief's punishment, he prescribes gold. And because it was indeed given by him to the other out of a lack of suspicion of theft—thinking, "How could this man be a thief, since he did not take it himself?"—the word "theft" (*steya*) is employed to dispel such doubt. Even though there is the status of a thief, the scriptural fine of gold applies; however, in other legal proceedings, he is to be treated like a thief. 8.213.
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages. (8.214)

The first half concludes the preceding discussion on disputes; the second half introduces what is about to be said. This is declared to be the non-withdrawal of what has been given. "Withdrawal" (*apakriyā*) means the loss of an action; its negation is expressed by the particle *nañ*. Thus, the gift does not become unstable. The meaning is that this alone constitutes stability in giving. It is "righteous" (*dharmyā*) because it does not depart from the Dharma. One should not raise the doubt: "How can the Dharma not be seen when, after having promised, one does not give? On the contrary, this is precisely the Dharma here: that one does not give, or that what has been given is taken back. "Declared" (*uditā*) means spoken. The compound word *yathāvat* itself functions in the sense of "according to reality. The meaning is "properly determined. Alternatively, the word *yathā* functions in the sense of fitness (*yogyatā*); the suffix *-vati* should be applied to mean "that which deserves such [fitness]. "Wages" (*vetana*) means hire; its "non-withdrawal" is the non-withdrawal of wages. This is the formal proposition (*pratijñā*): "The Dharma for those performing their own work for wages is now being stated. (8.214)
If one who has been hired, being not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as it was prescribed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid. (8.215)

One who performs the work for which he was assigned at the stipulated wage is intended here as a "hired laborer" (*bhṛta*). A hired laborer is one who has been accepted for a specific type of service. Having entered after saying, "Give me five *rūpakas*; I will perform this work for you within such a time," if he does not complete the work, he shall be fined gold *kṛṣṇalas* or [coins of] copper or silver, having taken into account the nature of the work, its duration, and other relevant factors. Furthermore, he shall not receive those *rūpakas* designated as his wages. If, being unafflicted, he does not perform the work as stated out of pride, there shall be both a forfeiture of wages and a fine for him who fails to work out of pride while afflicted by disease or similar conditions. Therefore, he is not permitted to say: "Give me an amount corresponding to the portion of the work that has already been done by me."
Some maintain that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should also be punished at their own discretion for abandoning [the sacrifice].

That is incorrect. For in this case, there is great harm to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) regarding his half-finished ritual; therefore, a severe punishment is appropriate here. Furthermore, they must be made to pay whatever has been lost by the sacrificer. They must restore the body through the consecration (*dīkṣā*), the *upasad* rites, and the divine vows (*devavrata*).

If another artisan undertakes any work—such as digging a tank or building a temple for a deity—and says, "I shall complete it for you; proceed," and then subsequently withdraws, he must bear all the master’s losses, expenses, and labor, according to the principle of the merchant and the porter. For this rule has been extended by Kātyāyana to all cases. If a merchant’s goods should be lost through the fault of the porter, that porter must bear the loss. Regarding Kātyāyana’s sūtra, "Or whoever else, having bound himself with money for someone's work, should turn back halfway," the connection is that "having bound himself"—meaning having pledged himself or caused the expenditure of money—if he turns back halfway, he too must bear that burden. This same principle applies even to one who works for wages for six months or a year, such as a *bhaktadāsa* (a slave for food). And Nārada says:
One who, having promised to perform work, does not do it; or one who, having been given wages, does not work by force;
or one who, having received wages, does not work—each such person shall pay double the wages.
One who abandons his work before the time is complete deserves the loss of his wages. (NSm 6.5–6; 8.215)

Punishment and the withholding of wages have been prescribed for one who is not in distress; now that which concerns one in distress is stated: "But he who, being in distress, should perform the work as agreed from the beginning, shall receive his wages even after a long period of time. (8.216)

If a laborer who has been hired while afflicted by illness should leave after his work is half-finished, he shall, upon returning once he is healthy, perform that remaining work as originally stipulated; even after a long time, having returned free from affliction, he shall indeed receive his wages for the remainder of the work performed. (8.216)
As it has been said: "Whether he is distressed or in good health, if one does not have that work performed, his wages must not be paid, even if the work is only slightly incomplete. (8.217)

Alternatively, if the master does not prevent it, and the person for whom that work was performed has paid his wages, then he should be made to perform an equivalent amount of work while in good health. Even if the master should say, "I have nothing further to be done," in that case too, the worker shall receive what is stated [in the law], provided he is not afflicted by illness. (8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate an agreement.

This is indeed the name of this legal point (*vivādapada*) concerning the non-payment of wages; therefore, this objection is not valid. How can it be said that this is an act of non-payment of wages when it is also stated to be an act of payment, namely, "he shall certainly not receive the wages"? For a name is not contradicted by being associated with any related quality whatsoever. Indeed, not all the meanings contained in a sūtra are operative [simultaneously]. Thus, for example, although in the *agnihotra* there is an oblation (*homa*) to both Agni and Prajāpati, the name "agnihotra" still applies. This has been stated in that very same work regarding the pillar and the mirror: "and that which is level and low... [and so forth].

*Samaya* means an agreement or convention: the undertaking that "this must certainly be done by me with your consent. Those who break or transgress that are *samayabhedinah*. What was indicated by the phrase "and the transgression of an agreement" (MDh 8.5) is now being explained.
With the first half-verse there is a conclusion in the manner previously described; with the second half, there is an indication of another section as previously announced. 8.218.
A man who, having made a covenant by truth with villages, districts, or assemblies, should break that covenant out of greed—him the king shall banish from the realm. (8.219)

A village is a collection of houses; by this, the people residing therein are meant, for it is among them alone that mutual agreements (*saṃvit*) can arise. Likewise, a country (*deśa*) is a collection of villages. A community (*saṃgha*) is an assembly of living beings from various regions and various castes who follow a single common purpose, such as the community of monks, the community of merchants, or the community of those learned in the four Vedas. Regarding the affairs of villages and the like—for instance, if enemies from another village say, “Our village has not been largely plundered; they graze their cattle in our pasture grounds and lead away water, having broken its embankments—if this is your intention, then we shall not permit them to do so today,” and if, while we are thus obstructing them, there occurs a physical conflict with them or a legal dispute in the royal court, then in that matter we are all of one mind. But if [the villagers] remain indifferent, then those who agree, thinking, “Very well, why should they transgress the long-standing customs of the village?”—having thus incited [the outsiders], should break the agreement and either forcibly join with those very people or cease to be included among his own. Such a person should be banished and expelled from the king’s realm; he must not be allowed to dwell within his own territory.

In this manner, when one has entered into an agreement regarding such matters as the affairs of merchants' guilds, monasteries, or Brahmins, he must not transgress it. This penalty applies to the violation of an agreement concerning a matter that benefits the village or similar community, which is established by scripture and custom, and which does not conflict with the interests of the city or the kingdom.

Regarding the phrase "out of greed": greed (*lobha*) is the lack of independence caused by a subtle sense of personal gain induced by another village leader. However, for one who fails due to ignorance, there is another rule [as stated in verse 8.219].
Having restrained one who violates the agreement, the king shall cause him to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and a silver śatamāna. (8.220)

Having seized, restrained, and oppressed [the debtor], and having not allowed him to obtain a [favorable] time [for payment], he is to be fined. Those *niṣkas* whose measure is four *suvarṇas* are called "four-*suvarṇa* *niṣkas*. Although it was stated here that "a *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*" (MDh 8.137), nevertheless, observing other measures from another treatise such as "The wise say a *niṣka* consists of one hundred and eight *suvarṇas*," he specifies [the measure]. If it is argued that this is already understood through the very power of the etymological cause of the term (*saṃjñākāraṇa*), there is no fault, because this is a metrical work (*padyagrantha*).

Others, however, having formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word "great" (*mahā*) as the primary object, speak of three fines: one should be fined six *niṣkas* together with four *suvarṇas*. Thus, ten *niṣkas* are established. For the sake of establishing the *bahuvrīhi*, the sense of possession (*matvartha*) must somehow be applied to the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). Indeed, Devadatta is not called "Citragu" (possessor of brindled cows) merely because he is accompanied by brindled cows. And these three fines are to be joined as one, depending on the specific act, according to the rule "if [the acts] are three, [the fine is] one. This fine is an alternative to the penalty of banishment. (8.220)
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment against those who violate the agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. 8.221
And "among groups of castes" means those whose [cognitions] are subject to deviation regarding assemblies of various castes, whether of different or the same caste. This concludes the section. 8.221.
If, after having purchased or sold anything, one should have regret regarding it in this world, he may return that object or take it back within ten days. (8.222)

Regarding goods that are frequently bought and sold, which remain intact during the course of trade and do not diminish in value from their original state—such as vessels made of tin, copper, and the like, which have a stable market price—one may return or reclaim such unenjoyed items within ten days. However, for items that have few buyers and are sold by some only on occasions such as divine processions or festivals, and whose value is uncertain, the period for rescission is either that day or the following day. In the case of fruits, flowers, and similar things, the rescission must occur at that very moment. Furthermore, even after having purchased something, if one regrets it, thinking, "This is not useful to me," he should return it within ten days; the seller, in turn, should accept it back. If the seller regrets the sale, thinking, "I did not act wisely in selling this," then the buyer must restore it to him. This time limit applies to those residing in the same locality; for those residing in different regions, the return must be immediate.
Some maintain that this rule applies to objects such as cattle and land, but not to clothing and the like;
for in another Smṛti, a different rule is prescribed regarding merchandise. Thus Nārada recites:
"He who, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase..."
That [article] must be returned by the seller to the buyer on that very same day, provided it remains unimpaired.
"On the second day, the buyer, by taking possession, shall incur a third part of the price;
on the third day, double that amount; beyond that, it belongs to the buyer alone. (NSm 9.2–3)

That substance which is for the purpose of sale is *paṇya*; having sold that, a person engages in transactions—such as the purchase of other goods produced by the sale—in order to acquire wealth for his livelihood. Furthermore, among merchants, such goods may be displayed on the marketplace or not displayed. In this context, a specific distinction is intended by the use of the term *paṇya*. Otherwise, only "having purchased for a price" would have been required. What, then, is this distinction?

It is said: when even that which has been purchased is sold by merchants without relinquishing its status as merchandise, then they purchase it solely for the purpose of resale. Regarding these merchants who buy from and sell to one another, some hold that the rule of Nārada applies, while for others, the rule of Manu applies.

What, then, is the correct principle here? One must follow the established conventions regarding commodities and the like. Thus, in the case of those commodities, commercial practice is established by such things as the assessment of the strength of horses or the mounting of hooks on elephants for sale. In cases such as deposits (*upanidhi*), if a cloth or other item is undisturbed and undamaged, the full value is given to the depositor once it is returned; however, the goods themselves are retained. But in this case [of a purchased commodity], even if there is only slight deterioration, the entire price must be paid back to the buyer. (8.222)
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the goods] to be given;
both he who takes them and he who gives them shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.223)

Beyond ten days, there is no rescission of a purchase. Whether it be the buyer or the seller who has developed a regret, if they dispute the matter before the king, both shall be fined six hundred [paṇas]. The prohibition "he shall not give" is not for the sake of some unseen spiritual merit (adṛṣṭārtha). What then is understood? Such is the established rule: after ten days, an unwilling buyer is not to be forced to relinquish the item, nor is the seller to be compelled to accept it back. Therefore, if there is mutual consent, there is no fault in either giving or taking back the goods. (8.223)
But for him who gives away a girl in marriage without disclosing her defects, the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas. (8.224)

If a maiden who is possessed of defects is neither disclosed nor revealed by her giver to the bridegroom, but is given away in this manner, then a fine must be imposed upon the giver by the king once the matter is known. The phrase "seizing [the girl] herself" is for the sake of emphasis. The defects of a maiden are those things which cause the obstruction of religious merit (*dharma*) and the capacity for progeny (*prajā*), namely: consumption (*kṣaya*), disease (*vyādhi*), and sexual intercourse (*maithuna-sambandha*). This fine is either the one mentioned in this section, "not [of] one who is insane" (MDh 8.205), or this present one. 8.224.
But if a man, out of malice, should declare of a maiden that she is not a virgin without showing any fault in her, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (8.225)
If one should say, "She is not a virgin," because of her conduct, sexual intercourse, or marital relations, and yet does not prove that defect, then he shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*.

Others, however, consider that because the fine is small while the insult is great, and because the suffix *-tva* is seen to denote frequency rather than a change in the meaning of the word's constituent parts, the specific verbal form "akanyā" (non-virgin) is intended here. The fine of one hundred is for him who insults her using this very expression, "She is a non-virgin.
But what is the distinction here?

It is said: he who speaks thus is questioned, "In what way is she not a maiden? If he should reply, "She is shameless, cruel, and speaks indecently; this is not the nature of maidens," and if he cannot prove this, then this punishment is applied when the denial of the maiden's virtues has been stated.

Alternatively, relying on the word *kanyā* as denoting the first stage of life, one might say to a man who is soliciting in her absence: "Is she not still a maiden, or is she too young or too old? If, after the maiden has been given away, she should inform the king that she was my most beautiful daughter and that he, while soliciting her, felt a desire for her; and if, having spoken thus, he is defeated—then this is the punishment for the one defeated when the time [of the marriage] has arrived. (8.225)
The mantras of marriage are established only for maidens;
they never apply to women who are not maidens, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites. (8.226)

Taking the hand is marriage (*vivāha*), which is the act of taking a wife. Because the mantras are present therein, and through their connection with the two [verses] beginning with "They have sacrificed to Agni" (ĀśG 1.7.13), they demonstrate the agency of these [mantras] in the marriage ceremony. However, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthatas*), it is enjoined in the rule for marriage that "one should approach a maiden" (*kanyām upagacchet*); the mantras express precisely such a meaning. It is not, however, because the word "maiden" (*kanyā*) is heard in the mantras that marriage is for maidens, since mantras are not injunctive (*avidhāyaka*). This very point is strengthened by way of a prohibition of the opposite: "Not among non-maidens, anywhere for men. In no Vedic branch (*veda-śākhā*) is a marriage concerning non-maidens heard for human beings. Those whose rites are lost—those who have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to religious duties such as the *agnihotra* or to the injunction for procreating offspring—are therefore not to be married. Consequently, it is stated immediately after the preceding verse that one who says "a maiden" when referring to a "non-maiden" (*akanyā*) should be subjected to a heavy fine: "A woman who has not reached sexual intercourse is called a maiden" (MDh 8.226).
The mantras of taking the hand are the definitive characteristic of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step. (8.227)

*Darā* means a wife; its characteristic mark is the marriage-mantras. By their employment therein, the sacrament known as marriage (*vivāha*) is accomplished. For the twice-born (*dvijāti*), however, there are mantras. In that regard, for a *śūdra*, there is the occasion of taking a wife, but he has no mantras; with the exception of the mantras, all other procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) exist for him. Therefore, the mantras serve as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sacrament called marriage. The completion (*niṣṭhā*) or conclusion of those mantras is to be understood as occurring at the seventh step. Having performed the oblation of parched grain (*lājā-homa*) and having circumambulated the fire three times to the right, the woman proceeds through seven steps, beginning with "This one, become a single-stepper," and so on, up to "Become a companion, a seven-stepper. Once she has stepped forward, there is no power of revocation (*anuśaya*) regarding the maiden's status either by the father of the girl or by the groom. Even if she becomes insane, she remains his wife; she is not to be abandoned.

However, this is not at all a marriage in the case of a woman who has already had sexual intercourse. Even though the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*), such as the offering of parched grain (*lājāhoma*) and so forth, may be present, she does not become a wife. Therefore, in that case, there is a right of rescission (*anuśaya*) regarding her just as there is regarding other objects. Furthermore, just as the *Āhavanīya* fire is not produced by an *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) performed by a Śūdra, and just as the essential nature of a marriage (*vivāhasvarūpatva*) is not established even when the fire-consecration (*agnisaṃskāra*) has been performed for a woman who is a *sapiṇḍa* relative; in that regard, it is well known: "By performing the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), one man becomes liable to penance. And according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, a girl [who has lost her virginity] is not to be married even to another man.

If one does not abandon a wife who has been afflicted by a disease causing sterility after having married her, what then is the recourse? As long as he possesses the authority [to remarry], he shall marry another, just as in the case of the rule: "But she who speaks unpleasantly [is to be abandoned immediately]" (MDh 9.81). However, once the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) has been performed and a son has been born, even if she should suffer from consumption or disease, he must not supersede her (*adhivindeta*), because the grounds for supersession are specifically enumerated (MDh 9.77–85). Even in that case, if this [supersession] is intended to apply to those who act out of mere lust—as in the rule "But for those who proceed out of lust" (MDh 3.12)—we do not forbid it.

In brief, the rule regarding a maiden is exactly like that for other goods: although for other items there may be a peaceful restitution even after ten days have passed, this is not the case for maidens who have been married. Even for those given for a bride-price (*śulka*), the rule for other goods applies prior to the marriage; however, for her who is given for religious duty (*dharmārtha*), there is no rescission at all, according to the scriptural statement. In that regard as well, the text says: "One may take back even a maiden already given if a superior suitor arrives" (YDh 1.65); thus, there is indeed a right of withdrawal until the seventh step is taken. But once the seventh step has been taken, because the act of giving is irrevocable—just like the gift of cows and other property—there is no taking back. Now, when a cow has been given by someone to another, there can be no mutual rescission of the gift and its acceptance through their respective desires, because the act of giving has terminated at that very moment. If, after having accepted it, one were to give it back to the donor, that would constitute a new gift; it would not be a rescission of the previous gift. Likewise, there is no renunciation by mutual desire between a qualified maiden and a qualified suitor, even before the marriage. Once the marriage is performed, there is no renunciation of the maiden even if she is found to be defective. A maiden who has experienced sexual intercourse is no longer a maiden and is therefore abandoned, since marriage is ordained as the defining rite of a maiden. And marriage is equivalent to the point of final utility. Just as a garment that has been worn is not returned to the seller even within ten days, so too is a maiden who has been married. Furthermore, this matter will be determined later under the verse: "A maiden is given but once" (MDh 9.47). (8.227)
In whatever matter one may feel remorse after it has been done, one should establish that person on the path of righteousness according to this rule. 8.228

This ten-day period of waiting is not merely the legal rule for the merchandise of merchants; rather, by means of this repetition—"in whatever [transaction]"—there is the inclusion of all undertakings, such as wages, agreements, interest, and loans, according to this ten-day procedure. "Dharmya" means that which does not deviate from the law (*dharma*). "Path" means a way. "The king should settle" means he should establish it. This is an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule: "when the transaction has been completed. However, when it has begun but not yet entirely concluded, there is a cessation of the entire process. For where there is a delay (*anuśaya*), and that [delay] is determined or established in the interim, there is a ten-day waiting period.

Furthermore, regarding a case where wealth has been brought for the purpose of increase, a priest has been chosen and a fee has been paid, yet after the agreement was made, a conflict has begun—some say that this is not dharma; for what has been done does not become undone.

And this which has been done is called "ceased," not "not begun. For this [usage] is not the *kta* suffix used in the sense of "commencement of an action" (*ādikarman*). Indeed, there is no reason to abandon the primary meaning [of the word]. As for that which has been done and yet is not considered "done"—even though it is done, because the intended effect to be accomplished has been frustrated, it is indeed "not done," just as food that has been eaten and then vomited up. Even regarding worldly matters, there is a systematic arrangement to be understood from the treatises (*śāstra*). In some cases, cessation and non-cessation are to be understood solely from the treatises. Furthermore, even if things have already occurred, a reversal is prescribed. Even when a loan of money has been settled and the coins have been returned to their place, they must be brought back [if possible], due to the lingering regret of one or the other party. Losses and expenses incurred when [the coins] were conducted according to the legal rule of the treatise must be borne. Likewise, they desire a monthly interest on those [coins] merely upon being received. Where such a pledge is made—"this [pledge] is to be enjoyed for such a length of time"—such a transaction is reversed within ten days if there is regret. But the selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is like the marriage of maidens; once the agreement is reached, one must proceed after ten days, provided this rule of the treatise exists. (8.228)
I shall now fully declare, according to the true nature of the law, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock. 8.229

Regarding disputes between owners and herdsmen—such as cowherds and others—concerning cattle and other livestock when a transgression has occurred, such as: "My cow was lost by you; give it back to me," whereupon the herdsman also contradicts this, saying: "It was not my fault"—I shall hereafter explain precisely and skillfully the true nature of the law and the specific legal settlement regarding these points of litigation. This introductory summary of the section is intended to focus the attention of the audience. (8.229)
During the day, the responsibility for reporting lies with the keeper; at night, it lies with the owner, provided the animals remain in his house.
Otherwise, if there is a failure in their security, the keeper shall incur the responsibility for reporting.

During the day, when a fault arises regarding the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) of cattle—referring to such matters as will be mentioned later, beginning with "lost or destroyed" (MDh 8.232)—the blame and censurability rest upon the herdsman; therefore, he must bear that fault. At night, however, the fault lies with the owner in the case of those animals that have died by hanging or other such means. This applies if they were brought into the owner's house—that is, the herdsman brought them into the owner's residence. Otherwise, if they were not brought in by the herdsman even at night and remain in the forest, then the herdsman would be the one liable for the fault. This is what is meant: when cows under the charge of a herdsman eat someone's crops in a field or are killed by someone, the fault is the herdsman's; but if they have been handed over by the herdsman [to the owner], then the fault is the owner's. The term *yogakṣema* is used here figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to mean "non-acquisition and non-preservation," just as one might say "one with eyes" when referring to a blind person. (8.230)
What is this "security" (yogakṣema)? Therefore, he explains in detail:
"A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cows, milk the best of ten cows; that shall be the wages for a herdsman who receives no wages. (8.231)

A cowherd (*gopa*) is one who protects cows; he is a cow-keeper (*gopālaka*). He is sometimes supported by food and other provisions, and sometimes by milk. Among these, one supported by milk should receive from ten cows either the best (*varām*) or the least (*avarām*)—the latter being due to the elision of the vowel *a* in the *saṃhitā* text. This refers to a proportionate share for protection. One who has no other food should take the milk of a single cow from among the ten. By this principle, the wages should be determined according to whether the protection provided is deficient or excessive. Likewise, in the case of milking or non-milking cows, heifers, draft oxen, calves, and so forth, the owners should determine the share of the milk as one-third in some cases and one-fourth in others.

This verse is intended merely to provide a general indication; however, the specific arrangement of the place must be observed. [The rule applies] when a village cowherd, intending to determine his wages, leaves the cows [in charge], yet he does not milk the tenth cow without having obtained permission from the owner. Even one who is paid with food might milk [the cows] with the thought, "I shall exchange them for milk"; to prevent that, it is stated that [he must act] with the consent of the owner of the cows. One who proceeds without the consent of the owner is liable to punishment.

That [cow] is the one just mentioned. If she has not been supported by food and so forth, her support must be provided; this is the mode of subsistence known as "support by milk" (*kṣīrabhṛta*). A laborer engaged in cattle-herding does so for the sake of maintenance, not for the sake of merit.

Alternatively, one who takes the milk of a tenth cow according to his own will would be a thief. However, since this [taking] is permitted, it is considered his wages (*bhṛti*), and thus there is no fault. If it is argued that even here there is indeed a fault due to the owner's lack of consent, that is true; however, some small measure of punishment should be assigned. He does not become a thief. But in this case, he might be a thief or a misappropriator of a deposit.
This verse should be stated at the beginning; therefore, it is recited in some places immediately following [the previous one]. (8.231)
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it perishes through a lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall be held liable.

"Lost" means it has departed from the range of vision and is no longer known where it has gone. "Destroyed by worms": worms called *ārohaka* enter through the birth canal of cows and destroy them. "Killed by dogs"—this is mentioned for the sake of illustration; therefore, the same rule applies to those killed by jackals, tigers, and so forth. "Died in a difficult place," such as a precipice, a cave, or a narrow space between rocks—the herdsman alone must make restitution. "Deficient in human effort": "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) refers to human exertion. Since the herdsman is present there, his activity consists of warding off predators with sticks and other means. If [the animal] departs because he, despite being active, was simply unable to ward off a tiger or the like, or if some animal suddenly leaps up and enters a precipice with such speed that even one pursuing it cannot turn it back, there is no fault on the part of the herdsman. (8.232)
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay, provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time. (8.233)

If cattle have been stolen by thieves after the drums have been sounded and proclaimed, the herdsman is not made to pay for them. The proclamation is intended to indicate the herdsman’s incapacity [to prevent the theft]. If many thieves plunder by force, then the herdsman is released from liability, provided that he reports it to his master at the proper time—that is, at that very moment—at the place where the master is present. How is this known? Either at that location, or at the master’s place of residence. Even if the master is not personally present there, he is nonetheless represented by someone who, having informed the king or an official, pursues the thieves. The word “his own” (*svasya*) is used to exclude the king; for a master makes an effort to recover his own property, whereas the king, even when informed by the herdsman, does not do so to the same extent. Furthermore, it is difficult for the herdsman to inform the king; if he were to report it only after the thieves have already fled with the loot, he would indeed be at fault. (8.233)
When animals have died, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hair, bladder, sinew, and bile to the owners, and show them the branded marks. (8.234)

When cattle have died due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, the ears and other such parts must be delivered to the owner; the gallstone of cows becomes a powder within their horns. The *basti* is a specific part of the body. *Aṅkas* are the ears and so forth—marks for the purpose of identifying the specific owner. These too must be shown. In this way, the keeper is cleared of liability. For by showing the marks, recognition occurs that "this is that very animal. (8.234)
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman. (8.235)

"Goats and sheep" refers to goats and sheep. "Sheep" (*avī*) means ewes and lambs. When these are hemmed in or besieged by wolves, jackals, and the like, and are not killed at the very first onset; and while there is this interval for rescue, they are not killed because no protector comes to release them; and since the protector does not come—that is, does not arrive—and the wolf kills them there by force, having overcome them with might, that fault belongs to the keeper. He must cause the owner to pay [the price], and he must perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Because a cow is large, it cannot be hemmed in by a jackal; therefore, the term "goats and sheep" is used, but it is not intended to refer to those specific animals alone. Consequently, this same rule applies to young calves as well. (8.235)
If, among those cows being kept and grazing together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (8.236)

Regarding the term *ajāvikāḥ* [105]: in the preceding verse, the dual number was used with reference to the species (*jāti*). Because it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of two types of animals, its singular collective form is optional. Here, however, the plural reference *tāsām* (of them) is made with reference to the individual animals (*vyakti*). If a wolf, having emerged from some thicket (*kuñja*) by means of a sequence of moving and leaping, should kill those goats and sheep that are confined—meaning they have been placed together in one location, gathered as a herd, their movement restricted from all directions and intermediate points, grazing in the forest and coming within the range of sight—the herdsman does not incur blame. For it is impossible to make a forest dense with many trees, shrubs, reeds, and creepers free of gaps, and wolves follow through such openings. Furthermore, because of the mention of "together" (*mithas*), if they are killed while at an extreme distance from one another, there is indeed blame. Since it is already established that if animals under the charge of a herdsman incur blame due to his negligence, that blame must be remedied by the herdsman himself, this detailed explanation is provided for the sake of easy understanding. (8.236)
The common land surrounding a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or else three throws of a wooden pin; for a city, however, it shall be triple that amount. 8.237.

A bow consists of four cubits; one hundred [bows] is four hundred cubits. This perimeter for the village must be established on all four sides. Land where crops have not been sown should be set aside for the easy movement of livestock. A *śamyā* is a wooden staff or pole; it should be thrown with the force of an arm, and from the spot where it falls, it should be picked up and thrown again, repeating this three times—the extent of that range, or the distance of the *śamyā*-throw, constitutes the boundary. For a city, it is triple that amount. "Village" and "city" are well-known terms. The throws of the *śamyā* refer to the exhaustion of its momentum upon reaching the ground at the point of impact. (8.237)
If cattle should destroy unenclosed grain there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals. (8.238)

In that case, one must not cultivate a field on pasture land. If it has been cultivated, then the means of subsistence [for the herdsman] has not been provided. Therefore, the fault lies solely with the owners of the field, not with the herdsmen. For a herdsman cannot lead each individual animal away by binding it with his hand, nor is there any other way for the cattle to escape. (8.238)
One should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it;
one must eliminate every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass. (8.239)

The arrangement of thorny branches and the like as a perimeter for fields, groves, and so forth, intended to prevent the entry of cattle, is called a *vṛti*. That which is commonly known in some places as *parṇikā* is a fence (*vāraṇā*) that serves as a barrier (*vṛti*). Its height should be made such that even a camel cannot look over it. Is the word "camel" used here in the sense of the second case (*dvitīyā*) functioning as the third case (*tṛtīyā*)? We say: no.
How then does the camel not see the enclosure?
Because he does not see the second side of the very high wall, the enclosure remains unseen.

And the opening or gap should block everything. That which is followed by the mouth of a dog or a pig is of the size of that mouth; one should act in such a way that the dog’s or pig’s mouth does not fit through. The meaning is that the opening should be even smaller than that mouth. (8.239)
Likewise, when an enclosure has been made:

"If a field is enclosed along a path or near a village, the owner, if he has a herdsman, deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for allowing cattle to enter; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unherded. (8.240)

On a path that is enclosed, in a field situated near a village, or within the boundaries of an exclusion zone (*parīhāra*)—the word "within" (*anta*) here signifies proximity—if an animal should eat [the crops], provided it is accompanied by its keeper, and the keeper is present; since a fine for the animal is impossible, the keeper shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. Even when the keeper is not present at home, if he is neither a well-known keeper nor a watchman (*vārika*) sent by him whose wages consist of a mere coin (*rūpaka*), then the ownerless animals must be warded off by means of sticks and the like, but they are not to be fined. By "ownerless" are meant such things as bulls set loose for breeding; however, for other ownerless animals, the fine falls upon the owner.

Alternatively, there is a *praśleṣa* (conjunction) with the word *aparivṛte*. And because of the connection with the field, the owner of the field—who is understood [to be present]—is construed as the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) in the phrase "together with the keeper" (*sahapālena*).

Who is to be punished in the case of a field? Both are to be punished: the keeper and the owner of the field. First of all, why indeed did the owner not construct a fence around the field on the path? And by the keeper, even though a fence existed, why was the field allowed to be grazed? One should restrain a cow that is without a keeper or one that has strayed from the herd through negligence. Thus says Gautama: "In the case of an unfenced field on a path, [the fault lies with] both the keeper and the owner of the field" (GDh 12.21). 8.240.
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule. (8.241)
Fields other than those situated along roads, fields, or on the outskirts of villages—when cattle eat from these, the fine is one *paṇa* and a quarter.

Now, one might argue that in this case there ought to be a smaller fine, since the field is closer than a distant one. However, when the field extends beyond the road or outside the village, a heavy fine is appropriate; for why would the cowherd allow the cattle to go there?

This is not a fault. If a heavy penalty were not prescribed here, then the fields of neighboring villages would be ruined by the cattle grazing as they enter and exit every day. However, out of fear of a severe punishment, people guard them with great care. In other cases, for one who leads the cows elsewhere for the sake of a particular kind of grass, the penalty is slight. Even in this case, there must be a prohibition against those who have no herdsman. In all instances, the owner of the field must receive the full produce; and these [penalties] have been determined by experts according to the specific measure.

“Of the field-owner” (*kṣetrika*): [the term is derived] from the sense that he possesses a field (*kṣetra*), with the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule for words beginning with *vrīhi*. This is the *dhāraṇā*; the meaning is that this is the settled conclusion. And because of the inclusion of the word “all,” even when the animal is without a keeper, the field-owner receives compensation for the damage. Although the word “animal” (*paśu*) is a general term applicable to buffaloes, goats, sheep, camels, donkeys, and so forth, nevertheless, based on the observation of other legal codes (*smṛti*), it is understood that this penalty applies specifically to cows. Thus says Gautama: “Ten [paṇas] for a horse or a buffalo; two for goats or sheep” (GDh 12.24–25); such is the determination in other cases. 8.241.
An exception to this is stated here:
"Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved within ten days, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods—whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper. (8.242)

There is an offense regarding buffaloes and the like because they are included under the term "cattle" (*go*). Bulls (*vṛṣa*) are oxen (*ukṣan*). "Sacred animals" (*devapaśu*) refers to those intended for sacrifice by a patron (*yajamāna*) and thus proximate to the ritual; or alternatively, they are called "deities" when they are images of elephants, lions, and so forth, established upon altars made of bricks and other materials. Their "animals" are those released by someone in dedication to them. For in that case, since a relationship of owner and owned exists between the deities and the animals, and a relationship of human ownership is impossible, this rule applies to those animals that adorn the temple precincts. However, it does not apply to those kept in temples by their keepers for the purpose of carrying loads, milking, and so forth; because the keepers themselves employ them for the sake of those deities, the keepers alone are the owners there. Therefore, the rule that applies to others who possess ownership is appropriate in that case. But those animals adorning the precincts which are unappropriated produce the purity of a sacred animal through their immediate proximity. Bulls released according to the injunctions for the *vṛṣotsarga* rite may be appropriated by some and thus become "with keepers," or they may remain unappropriated and thus be "without keepers"; for both categories, there is no punishment. (8.242)
In the event of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times his share;
for the servants, however, the fine shall be half of that, provided the landowner was unaware. 8.243.

If there should be a transgression, violation, or offense committed by the owner of the field on his own field—such as sowing at the wrong time, sowing unsuitable seeds during the summer heat, having his own cattle graze there, or entering the house without permission while the fruit is ripening, and so forth—then he should be fined ten times the amount of the king’s share that would otherwise have come to him. Now, if this was done without his knowledge by servants employed for the protection of the field or those appointed to guard the field, then the fine for the servants is half; such is the connection: "in the case of an offense by the servants, the fine for the field-owner [is half]. This has been stated here in connection with the subject of fields. (8.243)
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions committed by owners, cattle, and herdsmen. (8.244)
This verse is easy to understand. || 8.244 ||
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha when the landmarks are clearly visible.

Regarding the dispute concerning a boundary (*sīmā*), [the term *sīmām* is used] because it serves as the cause for the boundary. Since the prefix *prati* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* when it denotes a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a specific state (*itthaṃbhūta*), it can be said that even the cause is a characteristic. A boundary (*sīmā*) is a limit (*maryādā*), the division between villages and so forth; it is a measure, a quantity, or, in other words, a demarcation. "In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should lead [the investigation]" means that the determination must be made. He states the reason for determining this particular month: "when the embankments (*setu*) are clearly visible. Embankments are the marks of the boundary (*sīmāliṅga*) to be described later—specific types of boundaries such as clods of earth, stones, and so forth. Grass, *guñjā* seeds, and the like [are mentioned] because prior to this time, when grass has grown, no distinction is perceived between clods of earth, stones, and other soil. When grass is not recognized there at the spot marked by a stone, then that is determined to be the boundary. The same applies to the locations of creepers and so forth. Prior to spring, no distinction is perceived during the spring burning. And because he provides this reason, it follows that in whatever region they become manifest at a certain time, one must not allow any delay beyond that month. At other times, however, there is a need for time in order to recognize the marks; such is the purpose of specifying the month of Jyeṣṭha. (8.245)
And he should establish boundary trees—*nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *śālmalī*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and other milky-sap trees. (8.246)

"Pādapāḥ" means trees; "kṣīriṇaḥ" refers to those such as the *arka* and *udumbara*. These, because they endure for a long time, should be planted only at the boundary site, not in the middle of the village. If they were planted elsewhere than at the boundary site, they would not serve as determinative markers. (8.246)
By means of thickets, various types of bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and open ground, as well as reeds and clusters of kubjaka shrubs, the boundary is not lost. 8.247.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand— 8.248.
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed, having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries. (8.249)

*Gulmas* are shrubs with compact trunks. *Veṇus* are bamboos, *āragvadhas*, and so forth; the term "various" (*vividha*) is used because there are many kinds. *Vallīs* are creepers; *vratatīs* are long-stemmed plants of the grass family. *Sthalas* are artificial mounds made of earth mixed with grass and the like. The *kubjaka* is mentioned separately from the *gulmas* out of respect for it. *Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. *Aṅgāras* are pieces of wood burnt by fire. *Śarkaras* are hard clods of earth or gravel. *Kapālikā* is a fragment of a broken potsherd. The king should cause other hidden marks to be made once a new village has been settled, for the purpose of a definitive decision. In this way, the boundary will never perish; otherwise, someone might destroy that area through cultivation. (8.247–49)
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs, as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries. (8.250)

Large bodies of water are ponds; *vāpīs* are lotus-pools; *udapānas* are wells and the like; *prasravaṇas* are waterfalls or springs, which are areas of ground from which water flows slightly. *Devatāyatanas* are temples of deities, such as the dwellings of *yakṣas* and so forth. These are illuminating [marks]; for they cannot be destroyed with little effort, and if they were destroyed, there would be great sin. Furthermore, because all those seeking water and those seeking to see the deity are present there, the meeting point of the boundary becomes well-known to witnesses. (8.250)
And whatever objects of this kind the earth shall not consume due to their age, those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and on boundaries. (8.251)

The instruction regarding shrubs and so forth is for the purpose of illustration, not for the purpose of an exhaustive enumeration. Such types include the heartwood of *khadira*, black collyrium, and the like, which are similar to sugar and other such substances. What constitutes this "similarity"? To this he says: "Time shall not consume the earth. The consumption of the earth is used as a metaphor for its appropriation as one's own property. Just as that which has been consumed cannot be perceived separately, so too should one act toward [the land] as if it had become assimilated into the earth itself. (8.251)
By these marks, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties. (8.252)

When both villages are devoid of inhabitants, [the boundary] is to be determined by signs. When two people reside [in a place], it is by means of prior possession that is constant, uninterrupted, and whose limits are not forgotten—not by possession for three generations; for in this context, the authority of the latter is prohibited by the rule, "A pledge, a boundary... (MDh 8.149). Indeed, negligence is possible there because a boundary is common to many. However, for those who do not read the word "boundary" (*sīma*) there, the authority of possession is already established. Since the authority of signs has been stated, one might suspect the exclusion of other means of proof; therefore, it is stated again.
What is this "arrival of water" that is stated to be authoritative?

Just as other boundary marks are established at a new settlement, so too should the flow of water be made [a mark]. Alternatively, when two villages have that same arrival of water as the cause of division in one region, yet there is a dispute in another region, in that case, that very [water] is the authority. Or rather, this refers to the subject of a large village: if there is one bank of a river belonging to a single village, those on the opposite bank must not say, "Our land exists here as well. Or, even if some land is cut off from a certain village by such a flow of water, that very [flow] remains the cause of division in the case of a small amount of encroachment. (8.252)
If there were doubt even upon seeing the marks, the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely on the testimony of witnesses. (8.253)

But how can there be doubt when the markers (*liṅga*) are present? As for those that are concealed, if someone were somehow to come upon them and carry them away in secret to another location, there would be no certainty at all. Even those that are visible, such as the *nyagrodha* trees and so forth, do not grow only within the boundary; they are produced elsewhere as well. Therefore, because they are fallible, there is doubt. However, where this possibility does not exist, the markers are indeed authoritative (*pramāṇa*).

"Based on witnesses" (*sākṣipratyayaḥ*) means having witnesses as the cause; that is, it is where the conviction (*pratyaya*) regarding the witnesses resides. "Certainty" (*viniścayaḥ*) is the comprehension of the true state of affairs. The intended meaning is that in a dispute over boundaries, when the indicative marks are doubtful or non-existent, the decision is based upon witnesses. (8.253)
In the presence of the village communities and with witnesses at the boundary, the boundary markers should be questioned by both of those disputants. (8.254)

Even if a village consists of an incalculable number of people, nevertheless, when two litigants from two villages are at issue, the witnesses must be questioned in the presence of those two, as well as in the presence of other village families and groups of villagers. At the time of questioning the witnesses, all the villagers—even those engaged in their own business—must be present; neither the plaintiff nor the defendant is permitted to say: "In this dispute concerning our specific matter, why are these people standing by? Alternatively, if certain very elderly men from neighboring villages are designated as witnesses, other inhabitants of those villages must also be present. For what has been heard by them from the elders will not be contradicted when those elders are questioned in their presence. Regarding boundary marks: where there are marks on both sides, the determination of the boundary is made after ascertaining those marks from the elders. In the absence of such marks, one asks for testimony regarding the boundary itself: "What is the boundary here? (8.254)
But having questioned them, he should fix the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record the names of all of them. (8.255)

Whatever determination those witnesses may declare, all of them [should be recorded]; however, the rule regarding the statement of conflicting testimonies—namely, "in case of a division, [the word] of the majority" (YDh 2.80)—does not apply here. He should cause it to be bound [to the document], that is, he should write it down on a leaf; and the names of the witnesses should be written separately. 8.255.
Bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
they— impelled by their own past merits— shall lead you to the right path.

Taking clods of earth from the head of the broad earth, [the judges] shall be accompanied by witnesses who are adorned with garlands—wearing wreaths as appropriate, bearing red-colored flowers, dressed in red garments, and wearing red coverings. Although the root *rañj* (to dye) applies even to the production of other colors from white, its usage is most frequent for red, as in the expression "a red cow. This is intended to produce fear; moreover, those wearing red garments become full of dread. They are made to say: "Whatever merit has been earned by us, let that become fruitless. By the repetition in the phrase "each by their own," they should state their specific meritorious deeds, such as the giving away of a daughter in marriage or bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*). *Samañjasam* is an adverbial modifier of the action. They should lead [the litigants] along a path that is upright and righteous, not deviating from the truth. *Samañjasam* is an adverbial modifier of the action. It means a path that does not depart from truth, which is straight and righteous. *Samañjasam*, "straight" and "clear," have the same meaning. It is said that "clear" (*samañjasam*) refers to a legal proceeding conducted according to truth. (8.256)
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.

When falsehood is determined through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), through logical signs (*liṅga*), or from more trustworthy persons who testify otherwise, the punishment for each person is two hundred [paṇas]. This is because each individual acts as a witness, and witnesses are subject to punishment; for they do not give testimony collectively. Witnesses whose primary concern is truth—truthful witnesses—are purified; they are not bound by the sin of speaking untruth. "By what has been stated" means according to the facts. For there is no occasion here for speech consisting of mere words; rather, by this, agreement with other means of knowledge is indicated. Alternatively, it means "by the truth as stated according to the scriptures. For it is stated in the scriptures that one must speak the truth; therefore, it is said, "by the truth as stated. (8.257)
But in the absence of witnesses, four inhabitants living on the outskirts of the village boundary, being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (8.258)

The neighbors of the village and those living on the borders should be questioned; one should reach a decision based on their testimony, according to the rules for witnesses and not otherwise. The phrase "in the presence of the king" is for the purpose of completing the verse; however, the neighbors do not reach a decision by their own will as if they were the king. (8.258)

But in the absence of neighboring villagers, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests—those who dwell within the boundaries of the primary landowners and those who hold shares in the fields. (8.259)

The relationship of qualifier and qualified in the phrase "of the neighboring [deities] and the fundamental [deities]" is for the purpose of praise. Those that exist at the time of the establishment of the village—arising together with its origin—are called "fundamental" (*maula*). And those neighbors are permanent, because they are eternally present. Even their absence may somehow occur due to their disappearance; in that case, what is the recourse? At that time, one should also inquire about these [deities] which are about to be mentioned.

Alternatively, the original inhabitants who have experienced [the facts] are explained as the neighbors; they are the ones to be consulted in legal proceedings. In the absence of the aforementioned original inhabitants, the neighbors are the authority. In their absence, one should employ those who frequent the forests; one should question them skillfully. (8.259)
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers. (8.260)

These [people] wander through the forests; while traveling through the midst of a village, they might perhaps learn of that event. For as they travel by that path, having previously seen some men plowing a piece of land that was the subject of a dispute, they might ask: "What is this village that you are plowing? In such ways, a prior experience is possible.

Hunters are those who live by hunting; even for them, as they pursue deer that have strayed from the forest, there arises a connection with villages. Likewise, bird-catchers are those who live by trapping birds; in their search for them, they frequent all the villages. Cowherds wander here and there to learn about the specific types of grass [for their cattle]. Fishermen and boatmen, who live by digging ponds and such, go here and there, wondering where their work might be of use. Root-diggers dig up the roots of trees and the like, such as thick *kāśa* grass. Snake-catchers are those who seize serpents; for the sake of their livelihood, they too seek out snakes in various regions. Therefore, even they have many connections with people throughout the surrounding villages. Even the poor who subsist by gleaning (*uñchavṛtti*) maintain their mere livelihood by wandering through many villages, as do others seeking fruits, flowers, and firewood. (8.260)
Whatever mark they may declare when questioned regarding the boundary junctions, the king shall establish that accordingly between the two villages in accordance with the law. (8.261)

The construction is: "they were questioned according to the law. "Boundary-junctions" (*sīmāsaṃdhayaḥ*) refers to both boundaries (*sīmā*) and junctions (*saṃdhayaḥ*).
