A junction is the meeting point of two villages, and that is itself the boundary. "Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇam*) means an indicator. (8.261)
The determination of boundaries and embankments for fields, wells, tanks, gardens, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors. (8.262)

An *ārāma* is a grove or park, as well as a vegetable garden; the determination in this regard is based on the surrounding extent. This is stated for the purpose of excluding hunters and the like. A boundary-dam is a boundary-binding; it is that which is tied or established for the purpose of demarcating a boundary. [8.262]
If neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement. (8.263)

The fine for the neighbors is greater than that for the previous [witnesses]. The phrase "separately" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as the underlying principle has already been stated. Since those living adjacent to fields and other properties are necessarily aware [of the boundaries], their punishment is more severe due to their closer proximity. However, since it is not necessary for the neighbors to report the boundary of another's property, the fine of two hundred [paṇas] is to be applied here. Thus, at the village boundary, the fine for both the observers and the neighbors is two hundred.

However, those who, relying on the word "neighbor" (*sāmanta*), claim that there should be an equal punishment because of the neighborly status regarding the boundaries of villages, fields, and so forth, are to be disregarded due to their contradiction with logic. (8.263)
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (8.264)

This is stated in connection with fields and other matters. The mention of "fear" (*bhīṣā*) is intended to indicate any such motive. For one who steals while knowing that "this belongs specifically to him," the fine is five hundred [paṇas]. Since the context concerns the middle category of violence (*madhyama-sāhasa*), the specific mention of "five hundred" is for the purpose of establishing lesser or greater fines according to variations in the circumstances. Alternatively, some consider that the numerical figure in the preceding case was not intended to be definitive; therefore, one might steal by displaying intimidation, saying, "I shall have a legal document prepared," "I shall have the king punish [the owner]," or "I shall have the thieves blame [the owner]. In such a case, the fine is an alternative based on a different motive. (8.264)
When a boundary is impassable, the king himself, knowing the law, should assign land to some [of the litigants] on account of their benefit; such is the settled rule. (8.265)

"Incapable of being determined" means impossible to ascertain, due to the absence of characteristic marks or witnesses. The king alone, by his own will, should assign—that is, grant—the land, saying: "This land is yours; this [land] is yours. A knower of *dharma* must not show partiality toward anyone. This is what he says: "For the sake of benefit. By whichever boundary both villages become equally benefited—if, for instance, someone's land should be smaller, but their field is of excellent quality and highly productive, then the location should be considered in relation to that. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (i.e., it expresses "in view of"). That is, having regard for the benefit.

Alternatively, he may assign [the land] to some and take it away from others without certainty. If the disputing village is unable to define that boundary while others are capable of doing so, then he should assign it to those others; in this way, benefit is secured for himself as well as for many of the villagers. (8.265)
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse.

The meaning of the verse is that the former summary is presented as a concise restatement of what follows. Having stated "in cases of physical assault and verbal abuse" (*daṇḍavācike*, MDh 8.6), a deviation from the sequence might occur for the sake of brevity; namely, verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) first, followed by the application of physical force (*daṇḍavyāpāra*). However, since in a *dvandva* compound there is mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the meaning of the compound is understood even when its constituent parts appear in a different order. Because each member conveys the sense of both, the word "force" (*daṇḍa*) also includes the sense of speech (*vāk*). Thus, what deviation from the sequence is there? Accordingly, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* justified the commencement of the rule on "correspondence of order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*, Pāṇ 1.3.10) by relying on this very view, stating: "Because of the indication through technical names and compounds" (*saṃjñāsamāsanirdeśāt*, Kāt on 1.3.10–1). || 8.266 ||
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred; a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (8.267)

Harsh speech is verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), and it is of many kinds: speaking cruelly or indecently; piercing the vital points (*marman*); cursing; saying "May you become a *vṛṣala* (outcaste)"; causing suffering through falsehood, such as saying "Your daughter is pregnant"; and associating someone with major or minor sins (*pātaka* and *upapātaka*). Among these, this punishment applies when a *brāhmaṇa* abuses either a *kṣatriya* or a *vaiśya*. In other cases, the punishment is that prescribed in another *smṛti*: "When an accusation involving a cause for loss of caste (*patanīya*) has been made, the punishment is the middle amercement" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.214), and so forth. For a *śūdra*, the punishment—consisting of beating, cutting off the tongue, execution, and so on—should be understood according to the specific type of verbal abuse. (8.267)
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the penalty is twelve. (8.268)

*Abhiśaṃsana* means reviling in every manner; it is distinct from an offense involving a *pātaka* (a sin causing loss of caste), because a different punishment is prescribed for that. This [locative case in "vaiśye"] is a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*). The term "vaiśya" here is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). The punishment for the Brāhmaṇa who reviles, as well as for the one being reviled, has already been stated. However, regarding Kṣatriyas and others [reviling one another], one must consult other Smṛtis. Thus says Gautama: "Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are like Brāhmaṇas and Rājanyas" (GDh 12.14). In mutual reviling, if a Kṣatriya reviles a Vaiśya, he should be fined fifty [paṇas]; a Vaiśya reviling a Kṣatriya should be fined one hundred. Likewise, if a Kṣatriya reviles a Śūdra, he should be fined twenty-five; a Vaiśya [reviling a Śūdra] should be fined fifty. As for the Śūdra, however, a punishment dependent on his qualities will be declared in the case of reviling them. (8.268)
For offenses among the twice-born of equal caste, the fine shall be twelve [paṇas] for each transgression;
in cases where speech is not permitted during disputes, that same amount shall be doubled.

The mention of the "twice-born" (dvijāti) is not restrictive [to them alone]. When there is mutual abuse between persons of equal caste, the punishment is one hundred [paṇas]. Equality is determined by birth, wealth, kinship, age, occupation, and learning, since no specific distinction has been taught. Among those of the same caste, if the other is superior in wealth, the fine is double; if superior in kinship, it is triple; and so on, up to six times for one devoid of all qualities compared to one possessing all. "Vādas" (disputes), "ākrośas" (abuses), and "avacanīyas" (unspeakable acts)—the latter being extremely cruel acts directed toward one's mother, sister, wife, and so forth—these constitute the same base, but the measure of the fine is doubled. Because of the neuter gender [of the word *dama*], this [rule] applies as a supplement to everything, not merely to cases of equal caste. Alternatively, the construction may be "that same hundred," because of the force of the gender and because "hundred" was heard in the first verse. Therefore, even among equals of the same caste, the fine for unspeakable acts is two hundred. To justify the gender, the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*), though not explicitly stated, must be supplied. However, it is better to assume an ellipsis when the word "hundred" is already present. (8.269)
But one of low birth who insults those of twice-born status with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin. (8.270)

A Śūdra is of a single birth. If he insults or reviles members of the three higher castes with harsh speech associated with mortal sins and the like, or with speech characterized by cruelty and so forth, he incurs the penalty of having his tongue cut out. The statement "born from the lowest [parts]"—meaning born from the feet—is an expression of the reason for including even those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), since they too are indeed "born from the lowest," as evidenced by the prohibition of any other caste in the rule: "There is no fifth" (MDh 10.4). || 8.270 ||
But for one who pronounces their name or caste with malice, a ten-finger-long iron spike, glowing with heat, shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.271)

*Abhidroha* means reviling, a contemptuous thought: "O little Brahmin, do not compete with me! The same should be applied to other cases as well. *Grahaṇa* means seizing. One seizes a name that is either without an epithet or joined with a contemptuous suffix: "Devadattaka. By *abhidroha* means by anger; *abhidroha* is anger, censure, or reproach. Not by way of a wager. *Niḥkṣepya* means to be thrown down. *Śaṅku* means a stake or wedge. *Jvalan* means blazing, glowing with fire; *ayomaya* means made of iron. 8.271.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins, the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears. (8.272)

"This is your own duty," "this is the procedure here," "do not do this," "you are a follower of the Vedic texts"—those who, possessing only a fragmentary knowledge of grammar, are arrogant due to their pedantry (*dunduka*), teach in such ways; they are the ones subject to this punishment. However, there is no fault if one, out of affection or by relying on a Brāhmaṇa, being himself learned, should somehow remind [the student] of a forgotten distinction of place and time, saying: "Do not let the forenoon pass; perform the rite for the gods; satisfy the gods while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*); do not wear it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). "Heated" means causing pain through contact with fire. "One should pour" means one should sprinkle.
It is appropriate that it resides in the mouth, because one teaches through the mouth. What fault is there in the ear?
Its prior hearing of false reasoning and the like. (8.272)
One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas. (8.273)

Regarding what has been heard, he says, "This was not properly heard by him. He rejects what was indeed heard, saying, "That which was heard by him is not purifying. He calls one who prides himself on his lineage from Brahmāvarta, "This man is a mere outsider (*bāhyaka*). Likewise, he calls a Brahmin by birth, "This is a Kṣatriya," or he mockingly calls a Kṣatriya, "A Brahmin. He calls a student (*brahmacārin*) by his ritual action, "A graduate (*snātaka*). Regarding a limb of the body, he calls one who is physically unimpaired, "One with bad skin (*duścarmā*). "Vitatha" means falsehood or untruth. The instrumental case is used according to the rule "from *prakṛti* and so forth" (Kātantra on Pāṇini 2.3.18). Alternatively, *vaitathya* is unrighteousness (*adharma*), and its causality toward speech is entirely appropriate. Arrogance (*darpa*) is the contempt for others arising from pride in one's own qualities. There is no fault if it is due to ignorance or in jest.
To whom, then, does this punishment apply?
We reply: to all. Others, however, maintain that because of the context concerning Śūdras, it applies to the Śūdra alone, provided the falsehood concerns a member of the twice-born castes. (8.273)
Whether one speaks of someone as being one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly afflicted—even if speaking the truth—one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (8.274)

One who is deficient in one eye is "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*). One who is deficient in a foot is "lame" (*khañja*). Regarding such a person, or one with a withered arm (*kuṇi*), or one with a flat nose (*cipaṭa*), if he is addressed as "one-eyed" even when he is not actually so—by means of what is true, false, or by implication of what is untrue—the fine shall be at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*. If the fine is extremely small due to some form of favor being shown, then the minimum fine is one *kārṣāpaṇa*. Otherwise, depending on the specific individual, a Śūdra may be fined two, three, or five [kārṣāpaṇas]; or all [castes] are to be fined as previously stated. (8.274)
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher. (8.275)

"Slander" (*ākṣāraṇa*) is the sowing of dissension by generating hatred through falsehood. For example, one causes division by saying such things as: "This mother of yours is not affectionate; she has an excessive longing for a second son and gave him a golden ring in secret. In this way, one divides father and son, husband and wife, brothers, or teacher and disciple. The mention of the "son" (*tanaya*) is for the purpose of illustrating the second member of the relationship. Otherwise, if only "mother" were mentioned, the punishment would apply to one who divides the mother from the son, but not to one who divides the son from the mother. Although division is based on both parties, in common practice, the person through whose mouth the act is committed is the one who is to be divided. In that context, if the mention of the "son" were not there for the sake of illustration, then when one slanders the mother by saying to her, "This son of yours is disloyal and ill-behaved," the offense would apply only to the mother, and not to the son, as previously shown.

Others, however, say that *ākṣāraṇa* is the production of mental distress [in the teacher], such as saying, "I shall explain wealth or sacred learning," or "I am going to serve at a holy ford (*tīrtha*) and so forth. Because of the suspicion of such departure, a mental affliction arises due to longing; therefore, one should not act in this way.

Furthermore, as long as one's teachers live, one should not attend to another [teacher] nor act without their permission. However, regarding the production of anguish in the mind through inciting hatred and the like, one is not released from the hundredfold [penalty], because of the gravity of the offense according to the rule: "one who opposes the teacher" (MDh 3.143).

To falsely accuse a wife who is compliant and has borne a son of saying, "She is marrying another," is defamation. Likewise, to falsely claim that a virtuous son has been fathered by another constitutes defamation. For one who does not yield the path in every way to his teacher, the fine is one hundred [paṇas]. (8.275)
A wise king should inflict punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (8.276)

When a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya have mutually insulted one another, the construction [of the verse] is to be supplied as follows: "this is the punishment for those two. Alternatively, the dative case may be used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*): "the punishment is to be inflicted for the sake of their discipline. When an insult is made regarding a mortal sin (*pātaka*), this punishment consists in the infliction of suffering. (8.276)

In the case of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes, the application of punishment shall be exactly as prescribed, with the exception of corporal mutilation. 8.277.

In the same way, the first and middle *sāhasa* fines are extended [to other cases]. By that very sequence, for a Vaiśya reviling a Śūdra, the first fine applies; for a Śūdra reviling a Vaiśya, the middle fine applies. Regarding the statement "the infliction of punishment, with the exception of mutilation," this excludes the cutting off of the tongue which would otherwise be prescribed by the rule: "A once-born man [reviling] a twice-born man" (MDh 8.270). The phrase "toward his own caste" (*svajātiṃ prati*) should not be understood as meaning "toward one of the same caste. What then? It refers to the specific castes mentioned here, namely the Vaiśya and the Śūdra; thus, the term "his own" (*sva*) is used. This intention of the verse extends to mutual reviling. The term "toward his own caste" (*svajātiṃ*) should also be connected to what precedes. "Infliction" (*praṇayanam*) means setting into motion. For a Kṣatriya reviling a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the first half-*sāhasa* fine applies. Such is the rule for a Brāhmaṇa regarding a Vaiśya or a Śūdra. (8.277)
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault. 8.278

*Daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) is the infliction of pain by means of a rod; just as the touch of a thorn or the like causes pain to a person, the term *pāruṣya* (roughness/harshness) is applied here because of this common quality of causing pain. In that context, "decision" refers to the determination of the specific punishment. This verse serves to introduce the conclusion of the preceding section. (8.278)
If a person of the lowest caste should injure the highest caste with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.279)

The *antyaja* includes the Śūdra down to the Caṇḍāla; the *śreṣṭha* refers to one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). If one should injure him with any limb—either directly or by means of an intervening weapon such as a staff or a sword—that very limb of his must be cut off. "Injury" (*hiṃsā*) here means striking with anger, raising the hand or another limb with the intent to strike and letting it fall with force; it amounts to killing itself. The repetition "that... that" (*tad tad*) is for emphasis (*vīpsā*), so that it may not be understood that only a single limb is to be cut off (*ekatva-vivakṣā*). Therefore, if he strikes with multiple limbs, multiple limbs must be cut off. "Instruction" (*anuśāsana*) means teaching; this is the established rule (*maryādā*) composed by Manu. The inclusion of the term "instruction" is intended to prompt a compassionate king to act [accordingly]. (8.279)
Raising his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot. (8.280)

If one raises [the hand] and, out of anger, desires to strike that person's body, his hand shall be cut off even if he does not actually strike it. The mention of a "staff" is intended as an illustration for any instrument of injury that causes similar pain; therefore, a different punishment applies in the case of soft hooves and the like. Regarding the phrase "striking with the foot," the word "having raised" must also be understood here. This same rule applies even to one who merely threatens to strike (cf. MDh 4.165). || 8.280 ||
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be cut off. (8.281)

A Brāhmaṇa is superior by birth, even if he is inferior due to immoral conduct; the other castes (*varṇas*) are superior or inferior to one another in their respective order. In this context, the term “born of an inferior birth” (*avakṛṣṭaja*) refers to an inferiority of birth (*janman*); because of its proximity, superiority also pertains to birth alone. And for a Brāhmaṇa, there is an absolute superiority by birth, not an inferiority. Therefore, this is the punishment for a Śūdra who has ascended the same seat as a Brāhmaṇa. *Kaṭi* means the hip. There, a mark is to be made. Regarding the method of marking, it is not merely making a mark with lime, saffron, or similar substances, but rather for the purpose of proclaiming the punishment so that people may fear transgression. Thus, a mark that remains indelible in another country is prescribed by means of an iron brand. And so he will say later: “Having branded them with terrifying punishments” (MDh 8.352). He is to be expelled from the kingdom. *Sphik* is a part of the buttocks; both the left and the right. He should have that cut off, marked with the sign. Because of the rule of option (*vikalpa*), only that much is to be excised, not the entire buttock. Furthermore, the phrase “desiring to sit” (*abhiprepsuḥ*) does not mean merely by the desire; rather, it refers to one who has actually done so. This is because a mere intention can be denied, whereas the punishment is severe. (8.281)
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, he shall have the penis of one who urinates [upon him] cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him]. (8.282)

If one urinates upon another, or throws urine toward someone for the purpose of insulting them—even if there is no physical contact—he who insults by means of urine must be punished. This same penalty applies to this case as well, because the result is identical. Spitting refers to nasal discharge or saliva. If one spits into another's nostrils, the nose-cavity shall be cut off, because of the rule stating, "by whichever limb [the offense was committed]" (MDh 8.279). Farting refers to a contemptible sound from the anus. This is done out of arrogance, not through negligence. (8.282)
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation; likewise if they seize him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles. (8.283)

The word “out of pride” (*darpāt*) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. One should have the hands of a Śūdra cut off if he seizes a Brāhmaṇa by the hair out of a sense of contempt. Although the dual number is used, both hands are to be cut off even if he uses only one, provided that it causes pain equal to what would be caused by using both; it is not the case that only one hand is to be cut. *Dāḍikā* refers to the beard. Furthermore, for any other limb which, when seized, causes pain equal to that of seizing the neck and so forth, this same punishment applies in every case. “Without hesitation”: this prohibits the deliberation—which would otherwise be required by the subsequent verse—concerning whether the pain produced in the one who was seized is great or small; the punishment is incurred by the mere act of seizing. (8.283)
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished. (8.284)

This [penalty] is prescribed for mutual offenses among the twice-born (*dvijāti*), whereas for a *śūdra*, it is prescribed for an offense against a *śūdra*. He who merely pierces or tears the skin but does not cause blood to appear shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. The same applies even when blood is visible. Although blood is not seen without a breach of the skin, nevertheless, since a higher penalty might be expected due to the greater severity of the offense, the mention of "one hundred" is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
Others, however, say that this is stated for the sake of cases where blood flows from the ears, nose, and so forth, even though the outer skin has been pierced.

That is incorrect; for when there is a major internal injury, a heavy punishment is appropriate because of its magnitude. Therefore, where blood flows only slightly, the fine is one hundred [paṇas]; but in the case of a skull fracture, it is the same as for a wound involving flesh.

It has been stated that the word *niṣka* denotes a measure of gold. Regarding the phrase "one who causes the bones to be divided shall be banished," one should read it as a compound formed with a *ghañ*-affix, followed by the suffix *-kṛt*: "one who effects the division of bones" (*asthibhedakṛt*). "Banishment" (*pravāsana*) means execution according to the application of the *Arthaśāstra*, or alternatively, exile. For the hearing of the *Arthaśāstra* is observed in the context of the rules for punishment; thus, for instance, there is the usage "a fine of ten times the value" (*daśabandha*) in the works of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas. Exile applies to a Brāhmaṇa, not to others. (8.284)
In accordance with the degree of utility derived from all forest trees, so should punishment be inflicted for injury to them; such is the settled rule. (8.285)

The mention of "trees" (*vanaspati*) is intended to illustrate all types of immobile beings (*sthāvara*). For the injury or destruction of a tree that provides great utility through its fruit, flowers, leaves, shade, and so forth, the punishment is the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*); for one of medium utility, the middle fine; and for one of inferior utility, the first fine. Likewise, the specific location must be considered: such as the cutting of leaves, the cutting of fruit, or the cutting of branches. Furthermore, the specific nature of the fruits must be considered, such as their high value or rarity. Similarly, the specific location must also be taken into account: whether it is on a boundary, at a crossroads, or in a penance grove (*tapovana*). (8.285)
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain, one should inflict a punishment that corresponds exactly to the magnitude of that suffering. (8.286)

This is a specific detail regarding what was stated [in MDh 8.284]: "One who pierces the skin. If the term "human" were not used, this verse would apply to the injury of any living being whatsoever; therefore, this [specification] is intended so that there may not be an equal punishment for large animals and small animals, birds, or wild beasts. Just as it is said, "according to the degree of suffering": in the case of piercing or drawing blood from a living being, if the injury is slight and the animal is large, one deserves a fine less than a hundred [paṇas]; if the injury is great, even more than a hundred.

Others, however, [hold that] because of the mention of the word "great," the increase of the punishment is for the sake of great suffering, not for the sake of diminishing it in the case of a minor offense; thus, it is exactly as it was heard in the text. In that context, "striking for the sake of pain" means striking for the purpose of causing pain. However, there is no increase [in punishment] due to negligence. The two verses following this, beginning with "having fully understood the consequences" (MDh 8.126), should be explained by way of illustration. 8.286.
And in the case of crushing a limb, as well as [injuring] the vital breath or blood, he shall be made to pay the cost of recovery and expenses, or else the full fine. (8.287)

"Causing injury to the limbs" means by means of seizing them with tight ropes and so forth, or by dislocating the joints and the like. In that case, the assailant must pay the injured person as much wealth as is required for the recovery of the limb through the cost of wholesome food, a physician, medicine, and so on. This same principle should be applied in full to cases of injury to life or blood. Alternatively, the connection is that he must pay the expenses for the restoration of life and blood; by implication, this refers to those [limbs or vital functions] that have been impaired. "Restoration" (*samutthāna*) means returning to one's natural state. "Life" (*prāṇa*) here means strength. When a person is unwell due to a blow, his strength diminishes unless he takes nourishment, leading to emaciation and other effects. In such a case, once the limb has been restored and returned to its place, the assailant must be made to provide whatever is necessary for the recovery of strength, such as ghee, oil, and the like. Similarly, when blood is shed, or when the person becomes weak, or contracts another disease, the assailant must pay the expenses for restoration until the body returns to its natural condition. If the victim does not accept that payment, then the assailant must pay both that amount and the fine together as a single sum to the king. (8.287)
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally, he should provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king. (8.288)

"Substances" refers to household utensils such as winnowing baskets, mortars, jars, pots, pans, cauldrons, and others for which no specific fine has been mentioned. "Destruction" of these means their loss of original form, even if they remain functional. Regarding the phrase "whether intentionally or unintentionally," this refers to causing damage either through negligence or with prior intent, without distinction. One should satisfy the owner of the substance by giving another object of the same kind, its value, or by conciliation. However, one should pay the king the value of the substance or the substance itself. There is, however, an exception to this in certain cases. (8.288)
For leather goods, articles made of leather, and those made of wood or clay, as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value. (8.289)

Having formed a *dvandva* compound of "leather" (*carman*) and "leather products" (*cārmika*), there is a compound with the word "articles" (*bhāṇḍa*) as the substantive. Alternatively, having formed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) of "virtuous" (*dhārmika*) and "articles," there is a *dvandva* with the word "leather" (*carman*). Leather products (*cārmika*) are articles made from the modifications of leather, such as waist-bands, thongs, and the like; "leathers" (*carman*) are unmodified hides of cows and other animals. Alternatively, "leather articles" (*carma-bhāṇḍa*) are those consisting entirely of leather, while "leather products" (*cārmika*) are those covered with leather. Wooden articles include mortars, pestles, planks, and so forth. A clod (*loṣṭha*) is a modification of earth in the form of a stone—a mass of earth that has become solid. Articles made of that include small cooking vessels and the like. For the destruction of these, the fine is five times their value, and the satisfaction of the owner remains a necessary condition. (8.289)
They say there are ten exceptions concerning the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in all other cases, punishment is ordained. 8.290.

By this section it is demonstrated that even when injury occurs, in certain cases there is no fault. A "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to a cart (*gantrī*) or similar conveyance by which people travel along a road; and such carts and the like are drawn by oxen, donkeys, buffaloes, and so forth. Alternatively, those very donkeys and other animals, when ridden upon the back, are themselves the vehicles. The "traveler" (*yātṛ*) is one mounted upon it, such as a charioteer and the like. The "owner of the vehicle" (*yānasvāmī*) is the one to whom that vehicle belongs. In that context, if some property is destroyed or a living being killed by these [vehicles]—whether by the speed of the wheels or by horses and the like engaged in pulling the chariot—the question arises regarding the application of the legal principle concerning the transgression between the owner of the animal and the herdsman (*paśusvāmipālavyatikrama*). While it might be thought that in some instances the fault lies with the traveler, in others with the owner, in others with both, and in others with neither, the specific distinction not mentioned elsewhere is intended here; that is now stated. "Exemptions" (*ativartanāni*): that is, they proceed beyond the punishment for injury; there is no punishment here, meaning that the causes for punishment do not exist. Punishment applies to the "remainder," that is, to causes other than those already mentioned. Those others will be explained later. (8.290)
He first states those cases where there is no fault:

"When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or of the vehicle's wheel. (8.291)
In the case of the breaking of a yoke, a thong,
or a rein, as well as when one cries out "Get away!", Manu declared that there shall be no punishment.

*Nāsyam* means that which pertains to the nose (*nāsā*). [This is derived by] Pāṇini 5.1.6: *śarīrāvayavād yat*. It refers to the rope attached to the nostrils of oxen, the bit of horses, or the goad of elephants. When that is cut or snapped, or when the yoke is broken—the yoke being the wooden pole of the chariot—the term "one whose nose-rope is cut" (*chinnanāsyah*) denotes either the chariot or the animal via a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because both are connected to it, whether directly or indirectly. When a vehicle has arrived from the opposite direction, or is moving sideways or backwards due to some irregularity of the ground or the fear of the animals, the driver (*prājaka*) might somehow commit a fault, yet he would not be at blame. For a driver is capable of protecting those facing him; but how can he protect what is situated sideways or behind him while remaining out of sight? "Arrived from the opposite direction" (*pratimukhāgata*) refers to a return from the opposite side.

Others, however, say there is no fault when one is being harmed by an animal coming from the side while one is traveling straight ahead; they consider that to be "coming toward" (abhimukha). [They ask: why does one who has come toward [another] not yield the path upon seeing the one with the wheel?

The *akṣa* and the *cakra* are well known as the axle and the wheel of a chariot, respectively. *Yantrāṇi* are the leather lashings for the wooden parts of the cart. The *yoktra* is the wooden yoke-pin for the neck of the animal. The *raśmi* is the rein or hand-grip used for the purpose of controlling the movement of the draft animals. *Ākranda* is a loud cry meaning "go away" or "move aside. The particle *iti* is used here to indicate the utterance of words well-known in common speech to convey that meaning; however, this specific word (*ākranda*) need not necessarily be employed. If one does not deviate from the path while the driver is shouting "Move aside! Move aside! to draft animals that are out of control, and if [the driver] should cause injury, there is no fault. (8.291–92)
If a vehicle turns off the path due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for any injury and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred. (8.294)

The *prājaka* is the driver of the vehicle; his deficiency consists in being untrained (*aśikṣitatva*), not in negligence (*pramāda*). For if there were negligence on the part of a trained master, he would not be at fault. Therefore, if the draft animal or the vehicle should turn off course, leaving the clear path and going sideways or backwards, and should thereby destroy anything that has been lost, the owner is to be fined. Why was an untrained driver appointed? Because other penalties are prescribed according to the specific living being or the specific object destroyed, as will be stated later in the verse beginning with "In the case of killing a human, [the fine is] immediate" (MDh 8.296). Thus, the amount of "two hundred" is not intended here. Since the purpose of the sentence is merely to state the cause for the penalty, no other meaning is heard in the subsequent portion by which this sentence could be said to be a prescription for a specific number. (MDh 8.293–94)
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause the death of a living being, the punishment in that case is not to be deliberated upon. (8.295)

The punishment for injury has been stated. To explain a specific detail therein, he says this: If that charioteer, being obstructed on the road by another vehicle approaching from behind—his progress thus blocked—if, due to lack of training or negligence, he urges the draft animals forward with speed and fails to steady them again when a nearby chariot causes a sudden stop to his momentum, and if, due to that forceful impact, he kills living beings such as humans or other creatures with the yoked animals (horses, etc.), the chariot, or parts of the chariot, then there is no deliberation regarding punishment; the punishment remains exactly as prescribed.

Alternatively, horses that have galloped at speed on a road, upon seeing a chariot coming head-on as an obstacle, might be forcibly restrained and go off course; because they are situated on the side, they might strike those standing behind them. In such a case, no punishment is prescribed, because there is no fault on the part of the driver (*prājaka*).
Or else, "standing on the road" means being present [there], "obstructed" means not being restrained, and "vicārita" means specifically ordained or distinguished. 8.295.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediate and equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, it is half [the guilt]. (8.296)

If a human being is killed by the chariot or the animals while such a driver is in charge, then his guilt is equal to that of a thief; and although thieves are subject to punishments such as execution or the confiscation of all property, here only a monetary fine is intended, not death, because in the rule "in the case of large [animals], half [the fine]," only a half-fine is possible there. Furthermore, this has been accepted by some as the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*), since for small animals—those occupying the third rank—a fine of two hundred *paṇas* is prescribed for injury, and therefore, for those in the first rank, namely the principal [animals], the highest amercement is appropriate. "Living beings" (*prāṇabhṛtaḥ*) refers to those possessing life, such as humans, animals, birds, and so forth. "Large" means large in power in the case of cows, and large in size in the case of elephants and the like. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), donkeys, mules, tigers, and others are also somehow included.

We, however, say: he would have said "one thousand" [of the highest fine] if other punishments like those for a thief had not been intended. Therefore, because of the mention of "half," let there be no execution; rather, all the punishments for a thief mentioned previously—such as the confiscation of all property and so forth—are extended by analogy to these persons depending on the circumstances.

But surely, it is improper to extend the punishment for a thief to the killing of a human being, since that [punishment] was prescribed specifically for the slaying of a human. And that [punishment], as stated in "of men of noble birth" (MDh 8.323), is indeed death. Why, then, is it explained in this way merely to conform to the word "half" occurring in another sentence? It would be better to resort to some figurative application of the word "half" itself.

True, if the word "half" (*ardha*), being connected with "killing," could be justified otherwise; however, it is not possible for the word "like a thief," which has arrived through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), to have a different referent in the preceding and following sentences. (8.296)
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.

Those of small size are the minor animals (*kṣudraka*). Some of these are small by age, such as calves, young deer, and elephant cubs; others are small by their very species-nature (*jātisvabhāva*), such as goats and sheep. Regarding these, he will state that for goats and sheep the fine is five *māṣas*. This penalty applies specifically to those of small size among the remaining animals, such as cows and so forth. "Auspicious wild animals" refers to the spotted deer (*pṛṣat*) and others, both by their form and their characteristics. "Birds" refers to swans, parrots, mainas, and so forth. "Inauspicious" refers to crows, owls, jackals, and so forth. The word "animal" (*paśu*) denotes a four-footed species.

They desire this punishment for mere violence; they do not state it to be the cause for the procedure regarding vehicles. By the very statement, "In that case, the punishment has been deliberated upon" (MDh 8.295), the section concerning vehicles is concluded. "Deliberated upon" means that the deliberation is finished. Now, this is stated independently of that section. However, in the case of the rule, "In the case of large living beings, half [the limb]," the word "half" should be understood—based on another Smṛti—as meaning the amputation of a hand or other limb, and not death. (8.297)
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.

"Pāñcamāṣika" means that which has five *māṣas* as its measure. Since it is not specified what kind of substance the *māṣa* is, and because a middle-range assumption is appropriate, they say this refers to silver; however, gold would also be suitable. In this way, "equal to that" does not exceed [the limit]. But the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the specific type of substance should be determined in consideration of the consequences (*anubandha*) and other factors. (8.298)
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, these may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane. (8.299)

Those who have committed an offense are *prāptāparādhāḥ*. An offense (*aparādha*) is a transgression, a deviation from right conduct (*nīti*). When such an offense has been committed by them, they are to be struck. For even striking is called "harm" (*hiṃsā*), and that [harm] is prohibited by the injunction, "One should not harm living beings. However, this [prohibition] is set aside (*pratiprasūyate*) in the case of wives and others when an offense is the occasion. These are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*): whoever is someone's wife, and whoever is someone's slave, he is to be disciplined by that person. This rule is primarily concerned with the method for establishing [them] on the right path, and not merely a rule regarding striking. Therefore, verbal punishment and other means should also be employed. Striking may be used occasionally, in accordance with the nature of the offense. In place of "uterine brother" (*sodara*), "younger brother" (*kanīyān*) should be read: "the brother as well as the younger one. For he, like a son, is fit to be struck by the elder. Even a half-brother (*vaimātreyo*) is subject to this if he is fatherless and dependent upon a virtuous elder brother. He too, if he goes astray, must be restrained by means ranging up to striking. "Bamboo-splinter" (*veṇudala*) refers to bamboo bark. This is also an illustration; it includes other soft instruments of infliction such as thongs (*śiphā*) and the like. (8.299)
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief. (8.300)

By striking in a manner other than the prescribed place and means [mentioned in verses 284], one incurs the punishment for theft when using a club or similar weapon against the sense organs and so forth. This is a censure; however, this is not the actual punishment itself. What is meant is that the same punishment which applies elsewhere to the act of violence (hiṃsā) applies here as well. (8.300)
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.

This concludes the determination of assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), which has been explained in its entirety; it is the legal settlement (*daṇḍavyavasthā*). For the word *daṇḍa* (punishment) is used here in the title of the legal topic (*vivādapada*) as an indicator for the means of inflicting it. This verse serves as an introductory summary, stating: "Henceforth, I shall describe the various types of punishment for the thief, the robber. (8.301)
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase. (8.302)

A certain compassionate person, considering [the act] to be "cruel and harmful," does not engage in it. Therefore, in order to induce such engagement, an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the suppression of thieves is commenced. There is no fault of violence here; on the contrary, because it is a cause for visible benefit, the very act of harming the thief is conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskarī*). Furthermore, there are numerous explanatory praises intended to proclaim its equality with the Veda, for in that [Veda], the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśa*) generally consist of explanatory praises. By following the understanding of those [praises], the conviction arises that this matter is Vedic. Moreover, there are certain practitioners who are especially motivated by such praises.

One should apply supreme effort—that is, an excellent and extraordinary degree of intent. One should employ spies and carry out public measures with extreme diligence. "Thieves" refers to robbers. "Suppression" consists of restraint, execution, imprisonment, and so forth. When this is done, renown arises; it becomes established everywhere that "the territory of this king is free from affliction, thieves do not prevail there, and his prosperity is like that of heaven. Thus the kingdom prospers. The "kingdom" (rāṣṭra) is the inhabited country, and the people residing therein flourish when they are not harassed by thieves. Rejoicing in their wealth, even those living in distant border regions seek refuge in a kingdom free from affliction. Consequently, it prospers. (8.302)
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is perpetually characterized by the gift of fearlessness as its fee.

He who grants fearlessness—by preventing unjust punishment—to thieves and others, as well as to those under his authority, is always worthy of honor, even when he has fallen from his kingdom and dwells in the forest, even in casual conversation. A *sattra* is a specific type of sacrifice, such as the *Gavām-ayana* and others; for him, that [sacrifice] prospers and is accomplished. By the word "prospers" (*vardhate*), the author means that it possesses all its constituent parts and is endowed with such qualities. The meaning is that day after day he obtains the fruit of a *sattra*. Wherein fearlessness is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whereas in other *sattras* there is no such fee; this [gift of fearlessness], however, is superior to all because it possesses a fee. And since that fee is distinct from the usual fees of cows, horses, and so forth, the distinction from the ordinary *sattra* is meaningful. (8.303)
A sixth part of all merit belongs to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of demerit accrues to him who fails to protect. (8.304)

From all forms of religious merit (*dharma*), such as sacrifices and the like, performed by both village-dwellers and forest-dwellers, the king receives a sixth part. Likewise, even from demerit (*adharma*), a sixth part accrues to the king from that which is committed in secret by thieves. It is not only through the failure to protect those who are released by thieves that kings incur demerit; rather, demerit arises for those who steal as well due to their state of theft, and the kings become connected with even a portion of that, provided they do not suppress them. Furthermore, the very protection of those who are to be protected serves to prevent their connection with the fault of unseen consequences (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*). Therefore, it is fitting that a king who is charged with this duty incurs sin (*pratyavāya*) by failing to perform it.

But is it not improper [to claim] a sixth part of the merit because he has been hired for wages? It has been stated that there are those such as the poor, the helpless, and renunciants who do not pay taxes; what inconsistency is there in [the king’s] protecting his own duty in its entirety? (8.304)

Whatever he studies, whatever sacrifice he performs, whatever gift he gives, and whatever worship he offers—the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that by virtue of protecting him properly. (8.305)

What was stated as "from all [sources]" (MDh 8.304) is here elaborated upon. Study and the other [duties] have been made known elsewhere as being for the sake of *dharma* and are well-established in their form. "Worship" (*arcana*) means the honoring of gods and teachers. The word "of that" (*tasya*) should be construed with the object—the category of things such as study—since the word "action" (*kriyā*) is feminine. Regarding the phrase "a sixth part": it is not the case that the king receives a sixth part from the five parts of the fruit of the action belonging to the agent; for it is understood from the context of entitlement that the agent is the enjoyer of the entire fruit of the action. Rather, because of the inclusion of the term "properly" (*samyak*), this much fruit accrues to the king from the performance of his own duty. There is no transfer of merit or demerit performed by one person to another. It is an established principle that there is no fruit for one who is not the agent. (8.305)
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with fees of hundreds and thousands. (8.306)

Protecting all beings, both stationary and moving, from thieves, and executing those deserving of death according to the scriptures as they merit execution—the king obtains daily the fruit of sacrifices such as the Pauṇḍarīka, which involve hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees; this is a eulogy. (8.306)
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, shares of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell. (8.307)

Terms such as *bali* and others are names for taxes to be collected by the king, well-known in various regions like the word *sūpa-māṇavaka*. Among these, *bali* is one-sixth of the grain and so forth; *kara* is the collection of wealth; *śulka* is the share obtained from merchants; *pratibhāga* is the offering of fruits, tributes, and so on. If a king takes these [taxes] but does not protect [the people] from thieves, he shall immediately go to hell due to the exhaustion of his lifespan. Having taken the king’s share, protection must be provided out of fear of hell and the exhaustion of one's lifespan—this is the purport of the verse (8.307).
They say that one who does not protect but consumes [the people], taking a sixth part as tax, is the remover of all the impurities of the entire world. (8.308)

This is a supplementary deprecatory statement (arthavāda) regarding the preceding [verse]. He does not protect; he is a devourer (*attṛ*) because he subsists upon his subjects by taking their royal share. He clarifies this very point: "one who takes a sixth part as tribute. The learned call such a king the one who carries away—that is, accepts—as the entire impurity and sin (*mala-pāpa*) of all the world, of all his subjects. The meaning is that he is defiled by the sin of all his subjects. (8.308)
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who devours them instead, is destined for a downward course.

*Maryādā* is the established order of dharma rooted in the scriptures and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). He by whom this is disregarded or transgressed is a nihilist (*nāstika*), one who says, "There is no other world; there is no gift; there is no oblation. The first type has abandoned dharma through passion and the like; the second is one who possesses a perverse dogmatic attachment (*viparītābhiniveśa*) that "no such thing exists. He plunders—that is, he seizes—the wealth of his subjects by means of unjust punishments. One who is like him is a non-protector (*arakṣitā*). One should know him to be destined for a downward path; one should know him to have fallen into hell and to be headed for the lower realms before long. An alternative reading is: "And one should abandon a king who is untruthful. One should abandon him who says one thing but does another; one should not dwell within his realm. (8.309)
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by binding, and by various forms of corporal punishment. (8.310)

Having strengthened [the rule] with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), he now introduces the procedure for punishment. An "unrighteous person" (*adhārmika*)—by context, a thief—should be restrained or suppressed by three methods of restraint. "Restraint" (*nyāya*) means the act of controlling. "Imprisonment" (*nirodhana*) means confinement in a royal fortress or a prison house. "Bondage" (*bandha*) means the production of a lack of independence through ropes, shackles, and so forth, in that very same place. "Various forms of killing" (*vividho vadhaḥ*) range from flogging up to the destruction of the body and the loss of life. Although the number three is already established by the specific mention [of the three], the explicit statement "by three" is for the purpose of including other modes of restraint as well; by this, pouring heated oil and similar punishments are also included. (8.310)
